title: Mira and the Magic Circuit
markdown:
The wind outside Elmwood School was a chilly whisper. Inside the greenhouse a different chill had settled, the kind that makes petals think twice. Mira frowned at a small sensor in a moonflower pot. Sol the fox twitched his nose and thumped his tail against a watering can, which rang like a nervous bell.

“Still too cold,” Mira said. “Heaters on, and the temperature drops anyway. Look.” She pointed at a flashing red light. “It has stopped talking to the main system.”

The moonflowers needed steady warmth. Frost would ruin the pale petals before lunch, and Mira had already wiggled every wire she could see and tightened every screw that would take a turn. Nothing. Sol whined and nudged her hand, as if a fox could press a connection closed by hope.

“Having a spot of bother?” Dr. Imani Quill stood in the doorway in her crisp white lab coat, the sort of coat that made a greenhouse remember it was also a laboratory. She peered at the blinking sensor. “A broken connection, perhaps. For this gadget to tell us the temperature, it needs an unbroken path for its energy. A tiny road. If the road stops, the message stops.”

She picked up two thin wires and a small brightly coloured toy that hummed when it was allowed to. She held one wire to a part of the battery. Nothing. The toy stayed quiet, a sulk in plastic. “Energy has nowhere to go. The road ends.”

She connected the second wire to the other side, making a loop. The toy burst into a cheerful buzz that made Sol’s ears flick. “A complete path. All the way around and back. That full journey is an electric circuit.”

Mira looked from the buzzing toy to the sensor, then down at Sol, then at the pot’s rim. A tiny wire near the sensor’s base, barely a thread of copper, had slipped from its socket. She had missed it because she had been looking for a dramatic break, not a shy one. Careful fingers pressed it home. A faint click.

The red light blinked once and settled into a steady green. Numbers on the sensor climbed toward a temperature that would let petals stay petals. A sigh moved through the greenhouse that might have been Mira or the plants. The moonflowers unfurled a little wider, as if they had been waiting for the road to reopen.

“You closed the circuit,” Dr. Quill said. “A complete path for the signal. A loose connection stops the work because it breaks the flow. Not because the heater forgot how to be warm.”

Mira grinned. “A handshake electricity insists on finishing.” Sol barked softly. His tail, no longer a drum, swept a clean arc through the damp air.

She did not wait to be asked what else might be hiding in the wiring. She logged loose socket / toy-loop demo / green at last in the greenhouse book, left the toy on the bench still buzzing as a reminder, and let Sol inspect the moonflower pot as if he had personally invented sockets. The heaters, given a path that went somewhere, kept talking to the flowers. The wind outside could whisper. Inside, the circuit held.
